lineages.name: J Dilla
lineages.why: Disabled the MPC3000's quantise and hand-played beats, juxtaposing straight and swung time; lo-fi enthusiasts call him the godfather of the genre. He also used side-chaining and, by Questlove's account, added cassette-hiss samples for imperfection; Donuts (2006) is 31 mostly one-to-one-and-a-half-minute tracks.

lineages.name: Nujabes
lineages.why: Made atmospheric instrumentals sampling hip-hop, soul and jazz with turntables, samplers and drum machines, occasionally flute. His Samurai Champloo score (2004) tied lo-fi to anime, which the livestream visuals still echo.

lineages.name: ChilledCow / Lofi Girl
lineages.why: Dimitri Somoguy's channel began streaming lo-fi hip-hop on 25 February 2017 and made the looping study-girl animation the genre's image; it releases tracks on its own label. The stream format, with tracks programmed back to back, shapes the genre's short, even-level tracks.

name: Lo-fi hip-hop

notes.text: Kick and snare are slightly loose and rhythmically relaxed rather than locked to the grid — the unquantised feel D'Errico traces to J Dilla hand-playing an MPC — though less extreme than Dilla's own work.

Hats are swung by hand — first hat pulled back a little, second pushed forward, with small differences on each repeat — while the kick and snare stay on or near the grid; a second kick on the offbeat of each bar is common.
MPC swing percent is the share of the beat the first note of a pair takes: 50 is straight, 66.6 is triplet swing, 60 divides the beat in fifths.

Jazz-influenced extended chords — major sevenths, minor sevenths, ninths — held still in slow one- or two-bar-per-chord loops; one lush major ninth left for several bars, or two chords a step apart, are both idiomatic.

Many tracks have no dedicated bass — keys and kick carry the low end; when there is one it is a warm sub on chord roots, or a mellow line on chord tones with syncopation and octave jumps. No bass hand is named because the cited sources do not settle on one.

Acoustic piano is the instrument heard most on the ChilledCow stream; Fender Rhodes, nylon-string or hollow-body electric guitar through chorus or vibrato, occasional harp and sampled string sections are common.

Samples are aged digitally: high frequencies filtered off (Native Instruments' walkthrough low-passes from 3.12 kHz; bpmcalc cites 8–10 kHz), iZotope Vinyl crackle kept under the drums, tape wow and flutter on keys, 12-bit crushing for MPC heritage.

Heavy side-chain compression of the melodic loop to the kick is part of the aesthetic — the 'pumping', wave-like rise and fall D'Errico hears in Dilla and Flying Lotus — and can be more brutal here than in other genres.

evidence.inferred: absence in the two genre loudness surveys consulted (freshlybakedstudios.com, luvlang.studio), which report hip-hop and R&B but no lo-fi row

notes.text: No published loudness survey separates lo-fi hip-hop from hip-hop, so no LUFS range is given here.
Almost exclusively instrumental; the only voices are short speech snippets from film or TV, usually placed once at the very beginning or end of a track to set a mood.
Built in four- or eight-bar phrases, with elements brought in progressively over a short repeating loop rather than through verse and chorus.
Tracks are heard as part of hour-long mixes and livestreams, so they are short and flow into each other; Donuts, the model, has 31 tracks in 43 minutes and loops its last track into its first.

pitfalls.text: Low-passing so hard that drum attacks and consonants disappear; set the cutoff by ear against the unprocessed source and add one ageing effect at a time.
Crackle loud enough to be a part; keep vinyl noise as a low layer just under the drums.
Writing a rap or sung topline; the genre is instrumental, and a speech snippet at the start or end is the most vocal it usually gets.

progressions.text: The jazz turnaround, one bar each, looping.
The ii–V–I cadence, a bar per chord or two.
The four-chord pop loop with sevenths added.
Native Instruments' walkthrough loop (F – Am – E7 in A minor) with tension notes added.

references.title: Yawn

summary: Almost entirely instrumental hip-hop at 70–85 BPM: a looped piano, Rhodes or guitar sample with jazz-influenced extended chords over loose, unquantised kick and snare. Samples are aged on purpose — high frequencies filtered out, vinyl crackle, tape wobble — and melodic parts often pump against a side-chained kick, in the line of J Dilla and Nujabes.
